items.title: [Théoo] My phone is a noisy place
items.content_html:
A while back, I shared a note about how I had cut down my phone usage a lot and what it had changed for me.

And for a few months, I actually stuck to it.
But lately, I've been watching or listening to videos from the moment I wake up to the moment I go to sleep. And for the times when I can't watch videos (like when I'm walking in the street, for example), I will put a podcast or music to occupy the space.

I'm not sure why I went back to this sluggish state when I had been doing so well for a long time, but I think it's because I actually missed watching specific YouTubers and listening to specific podcasts. So I allowed some back into my life and then some more and eventually, it took over.

Which leaves me in a weird situation, because I now know that no YouTube at all is disappointing. There is some content that I actually like and don't want to stop watching, especially since it's only like at most 2 hours per week plus the occasional GeoWizard adventure.
But at the same time, I know that if I let these back in, I won't be able to stop myself, because there is a ton of content that I like, content that I wouldn't miss if I didn't watch it, but that is still nice to watch.
I could try an extension to hide the recommendations, but knowing me, I will probably deactivate it pretty quickly and find an "acceptable" reason why. Worth a try though, I guess.

The other thing that crept back is Spotify. I listen to music (or podcasts, but mostly music) when I'm not watching videos. On the one hand, it's great because I have discovered many new artists lately, but at the same time, I've been feeling more disconnected, irritated when someone is trying to talk to me and I have to remove my AirPods and, overall like my mind can never breathe.
I'd say that the thing that has changed since the last article is that now silence isn't weird anymore. I even enjoy it! But for some reason I always feel this need to listen to something. Plus, I have been questioning my relationship with music lately, but I will talk about it in another note.

Now again, I'm not sure about what the right thing to do is. I definitely don't want to stop listening to music, I enjoy it way too much. But I don't want it to be constant.
Trying to apply time restrictions won't work because I know that I will find "good reasons" to circumvent them.
Maybe something like "you can only listen to music when you do this and that" could work. This has worked for podcasts already, as there are some podcasts that I only listen to when cleaning and others I only listen to when grocery shopping.
Another idea would be to say "You can only listen to music out loud" and not in your AirPods. So that would automatically limit my time, because there are many situations where you can't listen to music out loud.

So where does this leave me? What about the things I said in the previous note about enjoying life without all this?
I guess it's as with all things in life, I need to find balance.

The approach to ditch all music and YouTube was certainly too extreme, but spending my whole days listening to stuff is also too extreme.
Another thing to consider is the fact that I tend to get absorbed by things, both the good and the bad ones.
So when I get to reading a book or programming something, I will just do it for hours upon hours to the point of forgetting to eat. But the same can be said for playing video games and watching videos, which has a much more negative impact.
And I don't know that I should change this, it's just a part of my personality, but I need to learn to put systems in place to prevent it for things that make me rot away.

I don't have a good conclusion yet. Honestly, I think that what would help me would be to have the opinions from a bunch of different people and see how they deal with all this, to try as many options as possible until I find the balance I'm looking for.

For now, I will try to limit Spotify and I will try YouTube "blocking" extensions. If you have any other ideas or want to share your experience, please email me, I'd be grateful to receive it.

I hope you have a great day, bye.

items.title: [blog.mastykarz.nl] Be honest about what your evals prove
items.content_html:
Your coding agent just scored 100% on an eval, and every criterion passed. There's only one problem: the code it generated doesn't build. How is that possible? The eval checked 20 aspects of the implementation. The agent used the right APIs and followed the expected patterns. It created the required files and included the necessary configuration. Every one of those checks passed, but nobody tried building the application.

The eval did exactly what it was designed to do. It verified the criteria it was given, and the agent met all of them. The problem starts with what we infer from that result. A 100% eval score means that 100% of the evaluated criteria passed. It doesn't tell you whether the agent completed the user's task.

The temptation of proxies

Ideally, an eval verifies whether the agent achieved the user's goal. If the user asks for a working application, you verify that the application works. In practice, that's easier said than done. Consider evaluating an agent that builds and deploys a cloud application. To verify that it succeeded, you'd need to build the generated code and provision the infrastructure. Then you'd deploy the application and exercise its functionality before cleaning everything up. Along the way, you'd have to handle failures and unpredictable outputs, sometimes for applications whose implementation you can't anticipate. A harness like that can take considerable time and money to build.

So we compromise. Instead of verifying that the application works, we check whether the generated code looks plausible. We inspect the files and configuration that the agent produced and compare its API usage against the patterns we expect. These checks become proxies for functional success, and there's nothing inherently wrong with that. Engineering is full of tradeoffs, and evaluating agents is no exception. Sometimes direct verification is impractical, and a proxy is the best evidence you can reasonably get. The trap is forgetting that we're measuring a proxy and communicating the result as proof of success.

Validation isn't the same as success

Agent skills show the same pattern. You can automatically verify that a skill's frontmatter is valid and that its structure follows the specification. You can even check whether the agent invokes the skill or whether its output contains certain strings. These checks are useful because they catch structural problems and regressions, much like linting or static analysis does in traditional software development. But none of them prove that the skill helps the agent complete the user's task.

Nobody claims that an application works because it passes linting. We treat static analysis and builds as different evidence from functional tests, and we validate performance and deployments separately again, because each of them tells us something different about the software. Agent evaluations deserve the same discipline. A skill that passes structural validation meets certain technical requirements. An agent invoking the skill is evidence that the skill was invoked. That's it. Neither, on its own, proves that the user got what they asked for, and even a comprehensive collection of proxy checks might miss the one thing that matters most.

What does your eval actually prove?

Before you publish an eval result, complete this sentence, and be precise about it:

When this eval passes, we know that…

If your eval checks implementation patterns without building the code, an honest answer sounds like this:

When this eval passes, we know that the agent generated code that satisfies our implementation criteria. We haven't verified that it builds or runs.

That's a defensible claim. What you shouldn't say is that the agent built a working application, because your eval never checked that. The same goes for the cloud application from earlier. An agent can generate infrastructure definitions and deployment scripts that look entirely correct, but until you deploy and validate the application, you don't know whether it works in the target environment. If a working deployment was what the user asked for, that's a significant gap in your evidence. An eval doesn't have to verify everything. You might deliberately accept that gap because direct verification costs too much, and that's your tradeoff to make. But the confidence you communicate should never exceed the evidence you've collected.

Don't let the nuance disappear

Imagine a team that reports consistently high eval scores. The results look excellent. Management sees progress that justifies the investment, and everyone believes that the agent experience is improving. Meanwhile, users complain that the generated applications don't work. How can both be true? Perhaps the eval scenarios don't represent what users actually encounter, or the criteria verify implementation details while missing functional failures. Perhaps both. Either way, the team has been optimizing against its eval results while gradually losing touch with what its users experience.

That's why a misleading eval can be worse than no eval at all. Without evidence, you know that you're uncertain. With a reassuring score that nobody fully understands, you might stop asking whether things actually work. So when users report failures despite high eval scores, treat that as a reason to revisit both your scenarios and your criteria. Your eval might cover different situations from the ones your users face, or measure outcomes other than the ones they care about.

Preventing this is primarily the job of the people who design the evals. They know what they measured and which compromises they made, so they also know what remains unverified. You can't expect everyone who reads the results to inspect the eval harness and reconstruct those limitations themselves. You can report them in a matrix of separate scores or in a short explanation. Either works, as long as the scope and limitations of the evidence travel with the results.

Be deliberate about what you measure

Proxies are often a practical response to how complex it is to evaluate real-world agent behavior. They're still compromises, though, and you should make them deliberately. Whenever possible, evaluate whether the user actually succeeded. When that's impractical, use the best evidence you can get and be clear about its limitations. Don't confuse validation checks with outcome evaluations, and don't let a perfect score imply more than you've verified. Before you celebrate your next 100% eval score, ask yourself: when this eval passes, what do we actually know? Then make sure that's also what everyone reading the results understands.

items.title: [Théoo] On techno-solutionism
items.content_html:
I've been seeing more techno-solutionist talk online lately. Maybe it's just my algorithms that decided to show me more of that or maybe people are actually talking more about it. Either way, it made me think about this subject and it's implications, and also made me quite scared.

When I talk about techno-solutionism in this post, I mean it in relation towards climate change. Here's a definition to make sure we're all thinking about the same thing when reading this article.

Techno-solutionism is the idea that we will fix the climate crisis by using technology so we don't have to change our way of life.

Now let me preface by saying that I personally don't believe in techno-solutionism and I will develop why in this post. But even if you believe in it, I think you should read-on as my goal is not to judge or critisize but rather to ask questions and I think your answers would be as interesting as anyone else's.

The solutions that are often brought up in techno-solutionist discussions are Carbon Capture, AGI that will find the solutions for us, Geoengineering and Nuclear fusion.
As of now, none of these solutions are a reality. We are seeing progress in each of them, but they still pose many challenges that we are yet so solve.

The question then is, do we want to bet on things that we don't know for sure will ever become a reality? Because, you might strongly believe these will someday exist but you can't prove that they will. It's just a belief.
Personally, I don't want to throw the life of future generations of living beings to a bet.

Now, let's say this works and we actually figure these things out! What tells us that we'll figure them out in time?

Because while we are working on these solutions, the climate crisis is still going on. Living beings are quickly dying and becoming extinct, and even if you don't care about non-human forms of life, humans are dying too.

Are we as a species really willing to let so many other forms of life die for us to keep up with our current way of life?

Are we, the people living in privileged countries willing to keep exploiting other humans for our own profit and well being?

And can we really feel well and happy about how we'll live in a world where we have "fixed" the climate crisis but can still feel all the damages it caused?

Maybe your answer to all of these is yes, and maybe you'd even tell me that it's also possible that we will figure techno-solutions in time.
So let's say you are right about this, let's say that by 2050, we've found solutions that allow us to go to negative carbon emissions!

Then the question is, are you willing to let companies decide of the quality of the air you breathe?
Because since we live in a capitalist society, the companies running carbon capture machines and doing the geoengineering required to keep our current living standards will want to make profit.

They won't do it for the sake of being nice to us, when is the last time you've seen a company just be nice and gain profit off of it?

Now you could argue that we are already trusting companies for many really important things like electricity or transport of goods. But these aren't vital things.
People used to live without electricity and they would grow their own food, but no one would be able to live without breathable air.

My personal opinion on this is that I am definitely not ok with putting my survival and the survival of future generations in the hands of any company. And don't get me wrong, I would love to keep up the life that I currently have, it's so comfortable. And I so wish that every human going forward would have the same comfort of life that I have. But I simply don't think it is possible.

Maybe you are ok with the idea that only a few living beings will have a great life at the cost of all others, in which case, business as usual is perfectly fine. But I am not.

I believe that it is more than overdue that we start rethinking our future.
I don't want of a future where machines are what is keeping us alive like we are some sort of ill person surviving only because of their ventilator.

Let's use what we know and are sure of to build a new collective imagination. A world where yes, we will have lost a lot of our current comfort at the benefit of more equality, more mutual aid, more connexion to nature and each other, more time to think and dream.
A world where we can wake up every day without being stressed by an imminent wall that we seem to being sprinting towards at great speeds.

Sure, we won't be able to eat McDonalds, order stuff from the other side of the world for only a couple bucks and get it delivered the same day, drive a car to go buy food at the big nearby mall, travel for a few hundred euros/dollars to go virtually anywhere in at most 2 days, change phone as we please, etc

But isn't that worth it for the certainty that we and other livings, will be able to live for millennia to come?

We should stop being trapped in our current vision of the world and I'm hopeful that someday we'll look back on this time period like we are looking back on how they lived in the middle ages.

I would love to hear about you opinion on this subject, even if you disagree. So please feel free to send me a mail so we can discuss this matter further.

Have a nice day :))

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] AI fear is driving employees to slack off, show up late, and even steal coworkers’ lunches
items.content_html:
🌾 🪶 ✏️

As more businesses adopt artificial intelligence, some employees—who are increasingly worried about losing their jobs—are starting to act out.

That’s the finding of a new study from Washington State University researchers, published in the journal Occupational Health Science, that looks at how AI adoption at work is affecting workers’ attitudes and behaviors in the office.

Research has shown that the increase of AI-based technologies at work—such as intelligent robotics, automated systems, and algorithmic management—may make employees feel insecure about their jobs and lead to more stress and less engagement.

Washington State University’s study looked at employees across 18 different industries and found that workers who had the greatest fears about being replaced by AI were more likely to behave poorly by, for example, slacking off at the office or even stealing a coworker’s lunch.

Researchers also found that employees who assumed they would be displaced were more likely to “morally disengage” at work, such as by coming in late for a shift or surfing the web while on the clock.

“Moral disengagement is basically a way of justifying bad behavior,” Tahira M. Probst, a professor of psychology at WSU Vancouver and lead author of the study, said in a news release. “We know what’s right and wrong. We know what organizational policies say we can and can’t do. Moral disengagement is a way of reframing that behavior as something that is acceptable.”

Researchers used the AI Industry Exposure index to identify which industries were most exposed to potential AI disruption. Workers in finance and insurance had some of the highest levels of exposure, while workers in agriculture, forestry, and construction had the least. Not surprisingly, the bad behavior was more pronounced in the industries with the highest amount of disruption.

The study’s bottom line: When employees feel their jobs are at risk, they may look at workplace expectations differently and rationalize behaviors such as cutting corners or undermining coworkers to protect themselves or compensate for what they perceive as injustice.

The findings also suggest that AI anxieties can hurt workers and businesses alike, pointing to the need for employers to be more mindful of how they roll out AI in the workplace so employees are better supported.
